Division B on ARCAP - ACA Counsellors and Psychotherapists


## Division A - PACFA Counsellors, Psychotherapists and Mental Health Practitioners


Certified Practising Counsellors Certified Practising Counsellors have completed an AQF (7-9) approved qualification of 400 hours of person-to-person counselling and/or psychotherapy training incorporating a minimum of 200 hours of direct instruction and a formal client contact placement which includes 40 hours of client contact with 10 hours of related clinical supervision within the training program. They undertake a minimum of 20 hours of Continuing Professional Development and 10 hours of Clinical Supervision per year.

Clinical Registrants Clinical Registrants have completed a further 750 hours of client contact linked to 75 hours of supervision over a minimum of two years and meet ongoing requirements of 15 hours professional development and between 10 and 15 hours of clinical supervision per annum.

Mental Health Practitioners Mental Health Practitioners are Clinical Registrants who demonstrate that they have met PACFA’s Mental Health Competencies. They demonstrate knowledge and experience of current assessment techniques and interventions in mental health, and an understanding of research and evaluation methods. Some of their ongoing PD and supervision relates specifically to mental health practice.

claim_bindings.claim_text: Their qualifications, approaches and services differ, so check each practitioner’s credentials and experience with concerns like yours.
claim_bindings.support_excerpt:
[source-09] A psychologist can help with assessment, diagnosis and treatment for a broad range of mental health challenges. They will usually conduct a series of therapy sessions, and may ask you detailed questions about your life, relationships, and wellbeing. They will use this information to work with you to develop treatment strategies and monitor your progress.

You will most likely see a psychologist following a referral from your GP. This is usually part of a mental health treatment plan, which allows you to access Medicare-subsidised sessions. Medicare subsidies are higher for sessions with a clinical psychologist than one who is generally registered. Clinical psychologists specifically train in the assessment, diagnosis, and treatment of mental illness.

Your GP will likely suggest one or more psychologists you can see, or you can find psychologists in your area through the Australian Psychological Society .

You can also see a psychologist privately, without a referral from your GP. In this case, you would not be able to receive a Medicare rebate to help with the costs. A private health insurance plan may cover some of these services.


## Psychiatrists


Psychiatrists are medical doctors who specialise in mental health. They assess your mental and physical symptoms to make a diagnosis, and work with you to develop a management plan for your treatment and recovery.

Psychiatrists help people with mental health conditions such as schizophrenia, depression, bipolar disorder, eating disorders and addiction. They can provide psychological treatment, prescribe medications and perform medical procedures for more severe conditions.

[source-09] While there is a variety of health professionals who could support you, it’s important to find the right fit for you. Just because you started with one person doesn’t mean you need to stay with them. Your health professional should be someone you trust and feel comfortable with, so take the time to find the right one.

Mental health professionals receive specific training and qualifications for their role. You can usually find the credentials of the professional you are receiving treatment from online.

referring you to a psychiatrist or other eligible mental health professional such as a clinical or registered psychologist, occupational therapist or social worker

claim_bindings.claim_text: Medicare helps with some eligible mental health treatments, but not every professional or appointment qualifies.
claim_bindings.support_excerpt:
A mental health treatment plan lets you claim up to 10 individual and 10 group sessions with an eligible mental health professional each calendar year.

To start with, your doctor or psychiatrist or paediatrician will refer you for up to 6 psychological sessions at a time. If you need more, your doctor will decide if they can refer you for further sessions. Health professionals set their own fees, so we may only cover some of the cost.

claim_bindings.claim_text: A treatment plan does not necessarily mean your sessions will be free.
claim_bindings.support_excerpt: To start with, your doctor or psychiatrist or paediatrician will refer you for up to 6 psychological sessions at a time. If you need more, your doctor will decide if they can refer you for further sessions. Health professionals set their own fees, so we may only cover some of the cost.

claim_bindings.claim_text: Ask for the session fee, any expected Medicare rebate and the amount you would pay yourself.
claim_bindings.support_excerpt:
To start with, your doctor or psychiatrist or paediatrician will refer you for up to 6 psychological sessions at a time. If you need more, your doctor will decide if they can refer you for further sessions. Health professionals set their own fees, so we may only cover some of the cost.

When you make your appointment, remember to ask:

how much of the cost we’ll cover.

claim_bindings.claim_text: Confirm whether the particular provider and service are eligible for the funding arrangement you intend to use, and what paperwork is needed before the appointment.
Ask about cancellation terms too, so you know what a missed or rescheduled session could cost.
Being able to book an appointment is separate from meeting the requirements for a rebate.
claim_bindings.support_excerpt: You can also see a psychologist privately, without a referral from your GP. In this case, you would not be able to receive a Medicare rebate to help with the costs. A private health insurance plan may cover some of these services.

claim_bindings.claim_text: If you hope to use private health insurance, check directly with your insurer about the exact service and provider.
Australian Government guidance on private health insurance explains that policies differ and do not all cover the same services.
claim_bindings.support_excerpt: Private hospital policies give you a choice of doctor and cover to be a private patient in a public or private hospital. General treatment policies cover treatments outside of hospital such as dental, optical, physiotherapy or pharmacy. Not all policies cover all services - check with your insurer to find out what is included on your policy and what you may need to pay for yourself.

claim_bindings.claim_text: Having extras cover alone does not establish that your proposed care is included.
Ask what benefit, if any, applies and what you would still need to pay.
claim_bindings.support_excerpt: Private hospital policies give you a choice of doctor and cover to be a private patient in a public or private hospital. General treatment policies cover treatments outside of hospital such as dental, optical, physiotherapy or pharmacy. Not all policies cover all services - check with your insurer to find out what is included on your policy and what you may need to pay for yourself.

claim_bindings.claim_text: Confirm the practical details that will affect whether you can attend: current availability, appointment times, online or in-person options and location.
You can ask these questions before sharing sensitive details about your story.
Use this message to ask about broad needs and practical arrangements.
You can leave out diagnoses, migration information, identity details and personal experiences until you feel comfortable discussing them.
Hello, I'm looking for support with [broad concern, optional] and would value someone who understands [language or cultural context, optional].
What relevant experience do you have, and how would you take this context into account?
Could you confirm your qualifications, fees, availability, appointment formats and any referral requirements?
Please also let me know how you handle enquiry information and whether you offer a brief initial conversation, including any cost.
I would prefer to discuss sensitive details in a session.
Thank you, [preferred name].
Remove any placeholders that do not apply, and add only the questions that matter most to you at this stage.
Ask whether an introductory conversation is available and what it costs rather than assuming it is offered or free.
Before sending sensitive material, check the practice's contact instructions and privacy information.
Do not assume that an ordinary email or enquiry form is confidential or secure.
If the information is unclear, you can ask how your message will be handled before sharing more.
Choose the questions that matter most to you, whether or not you share a cultural background with the professional.
You can leave others for a first appointment.
Listen for specific, understandable explanations rather than reassurance alone.
If an answer is unclear, you can ask, “What would that look like in our sessions?” These are conversation prompts, not a scored test or proof of clinical competence.

“What experience and training do you have supporting concerns like mine, including the cultural or workplace context that matters to me? Could you explain without sharing another client’s private details?”
“How do you find out what my culture and identities mean to me rather than making assumptions?”
“How would you take family, community or faith into account while respecting who I do and do not want involved?”
“What stays confidential, what exceptions apply, and who might receive information? If relevant, what would be shared with a referring GP or an employer-funded service?”
“Can sessions take place in my preferred language or dialect? If not, could a qualified interpreter be arranged, what would that cost, and how would privacy work?”
“If I say you have misunderstood my culture or something felt dismissive, how would you respond and adjust our work?”
“What approach would you suggest for my concerns, and how would we review whether it is helping?”
After the conversation, consider what felt understood, what remains unclear and whether the practical arrangements work for you.
You are deciding whether to continue, not making a permanent commitment.
Neither immediate comfort nor a shared cultural background proves that someone can provide the care you need.
Look for curiosity about what culture, language or faith means to you, rather than an assumption that your background tells your whole story.
Consider whether the professional explains their approach in understandable terms, acknowledges the limits of their experience and respects your choice to leave sensitive details for later.
If you correct an assumption, do they make room for your explanation and discuss how they would adjust?
You do not need to feel completely at ease straight away.
A new conversation can feel unfamiliar, so consider what they actually said and did alongside how comfortable you felt.
Pay attention if you feel stereotyped, if experiences of racism are minimised, or if the professional presents their own religious or cultural values as choices you should make.
Pressure to disclose more than you want, or dismissal of questions about privacy and feedback, are also concerns you can take seriously.
An unclear answer may need clarification, but repeated dismissal need not be something you accept.
If you want to revisit an assumption, you could say: “That is not how I understand my experience.
Could we revisit that assumption?” Their response can help inform your next decision, without guaranteeing that the concern will be resolved.
You can ask further questions, raise a concern or look for another professional.
claim_bindings.support_excerpt: While there is a variety of health professionals who could support you, it’s important to find the right fit for you. Just because you started with one person doesn’t mean you need to stay with them. Your health professional should be someone you trust and feel comfortable with, so take the time to find the right one.

claim_bindings.claim_text: You do not have to confront someone before seeking an alternative, and choosing differently is not a failure.
Use the reply to your enquiry to clarify missing information before deciding whether to arrange an appointment.
You do not need certainty about a perfect cultural match to ask a question, and an enquiry does not commit you to ongoing care.
If life is in danger, call Triple Zero (000).

claim_bindings.claim_text: Browse therapists that match your cultural background
claim_bindings.support_excerpt:
tal health platforms created with cultural competence at its heart. Connect with certified therapists and coaches who understand your culture, language, lived experience or religious beliefs. Whether you're looking for therapy in Hindi, coaching from someone who shares your faith, or guidance on intergenerational trauma, Tala Thrive makes sure you never feel lost in translation. It's support that feels personal, not generic - because we get you!
Who is Tala Thrive for?
Tala Thrive is for anyone from a diverse cultural background who wants support that already understands where they come from. Whether you have tried therapy before and felt unseen, or you have been putting it off because you did not want to explain your culture, traditions or family expectations to a stranger, you are in the right place.
How do I get started?
Getting started with Tala Thrive is simple and takes just a few minutes. Sign up on our website or download our app to create an account and complete our quick onboarding questionnaire, which takes ~10 minutes. Based on your responses, we will match you with the practitioners best suited to your needs. Review their profiles, select your preferred practitioner and time slot, and click "Book Now" to confirm your appointment. Still have questions? You can always email us at support@talathrive.com
Are the sessions virtual or in person?
All sessions are conducted
